aspect: The measured volume, and why it is an undercount
description: Between July 2022 and June 2023, 3,620 people were abducted in 582 kidnapping cases, with about 5 billion naira - roughly $3.9 million - paid in ransoms. The real figure is higher because many families do not report, fearing reprisals.
energy_note: Three and a half thousand people, in twelve months, that were counted.

aspect: The actors are not who the headlines say
description: Many kidnappings are carried out by amorphous armed bandit groups with no affiliation to Boko Haram or ISWAP, whose motivations are sectarian. Treating all of it as terrorism misreads both the threat and the remedy.
energy_note: Not ideology. A business with a catchment area.

description: North-east: Boko Haram and ISWAP. North-west: armed bandits using forest hideouts for kidnapping and cattle rustling. North-central: farmer-herder clashes. South-east: separatist-linked violence. Most of the country has a version.
energy_note: Four different threats, and a map with no blank space.

aspect: The ransom economy sets a price on a person
description: Families sell land, vehicles and businesses, or borrow at punitive rates, against a deadline. The asset base of a household can be destroyed by a single successful abduction regardless of the outcome.
energy_note: A family's entire capital, converted to cash, in four days.

description: She stops travelling that road by car. The flight costs eleven times as much and she takes it, four times a year, which is a meaningful fraction of her salary. Her mother, who cannot afford the flight, takes the road.
energy_note: Buying safety by the seat, for the people who can.

aspect: It reorganises where people will live and work
description: Jobs not taken, farms not worked, schools not attended, roads not used after dark. The economic geography of a country is rewritten by a crime statistic.
energy_note: A map of where you are willing to be.
